strengths: The paper investigates a relevant question: whether inexpensive representation statistics can help assess and improve language models.

The descriptive analysis spans several model families and three text domains, with generally negative correlations between dispersion and perplexity. Layer-wise, fine-tuning, and semantic-cluster analyses provide complementary observations.

The auxiliary-loss experiments report consistent perplexity improvements across three learning rates, with larger improvements in the mixed-domain setting. The appendix supplies useful hyperparameter and sampling details.
weaknesses: The model-selection claim is contradicted by Table 3. Section 4.2 claims Spearman correlation above 0.95 and perfect ranking of nine checkpoints, but the table contains eight. Computing the specified gap from its rounded values gives correlations of approximately 0.43 for Euclidean distance and 0.11 for cosine distance. For example, Distill-Qwen-1.5B has a larger Euclidean gap than Distill-Qwen-14B (2.73 versus 2.33), despite lower accuracy (83.9 versus 93.9). Within-size trends do not establish reliable ranking across sizes.

Section 4.1 demonstrates an association in label-constructed mixtures, not an operational label-free accuracy predictor. Resampling correct and incorrect examples changes the input distribution rather than holding it fixed. There is no held-out calibration, accuracy-estimation error, individual-error detection metric, or comparison with confidence and entropy baselines. A set-level pairwise statistic also does not directly define the proposed ranking of individual queries.

The kNN-LM application lacks an actual retrieval evaluation. Table 1 and Appendix B.3 report representation distances, but no resulting kNN-LM perplexities or comparison against an exhaustive layer search. Agreement with an attention-versus-FFN preference reported previously cannot establish that selecting maximal dispersion identifies the best retrieval layer.

The geometric interpretation overstates what the statistic measures. For unit-normalized embeddings with mean m, Equation 3 equals N/(N−1) times (1−||m||²). Thus it measures the normalized centroid magnitude and cannot distinguish a broad, high-dimensional representation from a balanced distribution on two antipodal points. Likewise, the cross-domain objective depends only on the dot product of domain means and can increase while each domain remains collapsed. Claims about discriminative capacity and avoiding rank collapse require additional geometric measurements.

The main correlations are computed after sorting by perplexity, averaging within bins, and selecting bins uniformly in perplexity space. These establish conditional aggregate trends, but not predictive accuracy on naturally sampled unseen data or comparability across models. Sensitivity to binning and controls for token frequency, topic, and final-token identity are missing. Low observed-token perplexity is also not equivalent to low predictive entropy.

The training evidence is preliminary: GPT-2-small is trained from scratch and evaluated only at 500 and 1000 steps, without seed variability, convergence results, or compute-matched comparisons. Comparisons against existing contrastive or isotropy regularizers, including the cited ContraCLM, are absent, leaving novelty and lasting benefit unclear.

Reproducibility gaps affect the practical applications: exact domain/reference token lists, consistent benchmark prompting and decoding protocols, and the Python-code dataset and split are unspecified. Switching from contextual cosine dispersion to output-embedding Euclidean distances also introduces norm and model-scale confounds that are not adequately controlled.

strengths: The empirical survey spans five model families and three text domains, providing useful evidence that perplexity-conditioned groups often exhibit a negative association between perplexity and representation dispersion.
The layer-wise, fine-tuning, and within-cluster analyses offer complementary observations about representation geometry during learning.

The auxiliary-loss experiments report consistent perplexity improvements across three learning rates, with particularly promising gains in joint text/code training. Appendices provide several training and measurement details.
weaknesses: The model-selection claims contradict the reported numbers. Section 4.2 claims perfect ranking of nine checkpoints, but Table 3 contains eight and substantial ranking reversals. For example, the Euclidean dispersion gap is 2.24 for Qwen2.5-1.5B versus 1.50 for Qwen2.5-7B, although their accuracies are 35.0% and 49.8%. Distill-Qwen-1.5B also has a larger gap than Distill-Qwen-14B despite lower accuracy. The cosine values likewise do not support perfect ranking. These discrepancies undermine a central application claim.

Section 4.1 demonstrates association in label-constructed mixtures, not operational prediction of accuracy without labels. Correct and incorrect examples are explicitly partitioned using ground truth before constructing each evaluation set. There is no held-out calibration or transfer experiment, accuracy-estimation error, or individual error-detection evaluation. Changing the correctness mixture also does not keep the input distribution fixed as claimed. Comparisons against confidence, entropy, and perplexity baselines are missing.

The kNN-LM application never measures kNN-LM performance. Table 1 compares dispersion for only two sublayers of the final block; it reports no retrieval-augmented perplexities, exhaustive layer comparisons, or selection regret. Agreement with a previously reported preference for attention outputs cannot establish that maximum dispersion identifies the best retrieval representation.

The geometric interpretation exceeds what the statistic measures. For normalized vectors u_i, Equation 3 equals N/(N−1) times (1−||mean(u_i)||²). Thus, it measures the magnitude of the mean direction and cannot by itself establish high rank, broad coverage, or discriminative information: balanced antipodal vectors can maximize it while occupying one dimension. The single-domain auxiliary objective therefore amounts to penalizing the normalized-vector mean; the cross-domain objective depends only on the two domain means. These properties require analysis and comparison with existing centering, isotropy, and representation-regularization approaches.

The main correlations concern groups selected by perplexity within individual models. They do not establish calibrated prediction across models or naturally occurring datasets. Perplexity-based binning and additional uniform sampling alter the evaluated distribution, yet sensitivity analyses and controls for token identity, frequency, and semantic composition are absent. The narrative also conflates low observed-token perplexity with low predictive entropy, which are distinct quantities.

Training evidence is preliminary: only GPT-2-small trained from scratch is evaluated, at 500 and 1,000 steps, without repeated-run uncertainty or convergence results. Single-domain gains at 1,000 steps are only 1.0–3.1 perplexity points. There are no competing regularizer baselines or evidence that the proposed geometric mechanism explains the improvements. Reproducibility is further limited by unspecified domain-token/reference sets, incomplete code-data details, and a blank code-availability link.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant question: whether inexpensive representation statistics can diagnose language-model performance and guide training or model selection.

The descriptive study has useful breadth, reporting negative dispersion–perplexity correlations across multiple model families and three text domains, supplemented by layer-wise, fine-tuning, and semantic-cluster analyses.

The auxiliary-loss experiments provide preliminary intervention evidence: Table 2 reports consistent perplexity improvements across three learning rates, with larger improvements in joint Wikipedia/code training.
The appendix provides additional plots, numerical results, and several training configurations, helping readers scrutinize the findings.
weaknesses: The model-selection claim is contradicted by the reported numbers. Section 4.2 claims perfect ranking of nine checkpoints and Spearman correlation above 0.95, but Table 3 contains eight checkpoints and clear reversals. Using the stated Euclidean gap, Distill-Qwen-1.5B scores 2.73 with 83.9% accuracy, whereas Distill-Qwen-14B scores 2.33 with 93.9% accuracy; cosine gaps also reverse this pair. Within-scale trends do not establish the claimed ranking across scales. Moreover, this application switches from contextual hidden states to output token embeddings without adequately establishing the connection.

Section 4.1 does not demonstrate prospective, label-free accuracy prediction. It uses ground-truth correctness to construct mixtures and then measures their dispersion. This establishes an association under selected mixtures, but changing the correctness mixture does not generally hold the input distribution fixed. There is no held-out accuracy-estimation error, transfer evaluation, or instance-level error-detection metric supporting the proposed practical uses. A set-level statistic also does not directly define how to rank individual queries.

The kNN-LM application lacks an actual retrieval-performance evaluation. Table 1 and Appendix B.3 compare dispersion at two sublayers, but report no augmented perplexities, datastore experiments, or comparison against exhaustive layer selection. Agreement with a previously reported preference for attention outputs is insufficient to substantiate the claim that maximum dispersion identifies the best retrieval representation.

The geometric interpretation overstates what the statistic measures. For normalized vectors u_i with mean m, Equation 3 equals N/(N−1) times (1−||m||²). It therefore measures the normalized mean's magnitude, not rank, dimensional coverage, or discriminative structure: a balanced distribution on two antipodal points can maximize it. Likewise, the cross-domain objective depends only on the dot product of domain means and need not improve within-domain discrimination. Comparisons with centering, spectral measures, and existing contrastive objectives are needed.

The main correlations are calculated after sorting examples by perplexity, aggregating them into bins, and selecting bins uniformly in perplexity space. These are useful descriptive results, but do not establish predictive accuracy on naturally sampled unseen sets or reliable comparisons between models. Sensitivity to binning, sampling, token identity, and text composition is not established. The explanation also conflates low observed-token perplexity with low predictive entropy, which are distinct quantities.

Training evidence is limited to GPT-2 small trained from scratch for 500–1000 steps, without seed variability, convergence results, larger-model validation, or comparisons to related regularizers such as ContraCLM. The results support promising early-training improvements, but do not establish durable generalization gains or the proposed causal explanation.

Important baselines and reproducibility details are missing. The diagnostic applications are not compared with confidence, entropy, or ordinary perplexity on unlabeled text. Domain-token and reference-token lists, the Python-code data source, and complete evaluation protocols are not specified. Together with the unsupported application claims and numerical inconsistency, these gaps leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold despite the promising descriptive observations.

strengths: The empirical survey covers multiple model families and text domains, providing substantial evidence for a negative association between perplexity and dispersion within perplexity-conditioned groups.
Layer-wise analyses, fine-tuning trajectories, semantic-cluster experiments, and the supplementary Vendi-score analysis offer complementary views of the observed relationship.
The proposed statistics and auxiliary objective are simple. Initial training experiments show consistent perplexity improvements, with larger gains in the mixed-domain setting.
weaknesses: The individual-example ranking claim is not demonstrated. Section 3.1 constructs batches using known correctness labels and measures batch-level dispersion; this does not establish a deployable per-example hardness score or label-free slice-discovery procedure. The supplementary query-perplexity comparison uses the same synthetic batches. Evaluation on naturally occurring slices, individual error detection, and answer-confidence baselines is needed.

The model-selection claims conflict with the reported numbers. Section 3.2 claims perfect ranking of nine Qwen checkpoints, but Tables 9–10 contain eight and show cross-scale reversals: Distill-Qwen-1.5B has greater dispersion gap than Distill-Qwen-14B despite lower accuracy. Even within a fixed scale, Table 12 gives Llama2-7B a larger cosine gap than CodeLlama-7B despite substantially worse HumanEval performance. The metric's dependence on distance choice and model scale needs explicit treatment.

The kNN-LM application lacks direct validation. Table 1 and Appendix B.3 report representation distances, but no retrieval-augmented perplexities or comparisons against an exhaustive layer search. Agreement with an attention-versus-FFN preference reported in prior work does not establish that maximizing dispersion selects the best retrieval layer.

The geometric interpretation overstates what the statistic measures. For unit vectors u_i, Equation 1 equals N/(N−1) times (1−||mean(u_i)||²), so it measures the normalized centroid's magnitude rather than rank or uniform coverage. Two balanced antipodal clusters can maximize this statistic while remaining one-dimensional. The single-domain auxiliary loss therefore encourages mean centering, and the cross-domain loss can favor opposing domain centroids without improving within-domain discrimination. The Vendi-score correlations do not resolve this distinction.

The main correlations are computed after sorting by perplexity and selecting bins uniformly in perplexity space. These are conditional aggregate associations, not direct evidence that dispersion predicts individual difficulty or ranks arbitrary models. Controls for token identity, frequency, content composition, and binning choices are missing. Likewise, the OLMo trajectory correlations do not establish predictive value beyond the shared trend with training progress.

The training evidence is preliminary: only GPT-2 small trained from scratch, checkpoints at 500 and 1,000 steps, no reported variation across training seeds, and no comparison against established contrastive or isotropy regularizers such as ContraCLM. The squeeze ablation shows that the opposite regularizer can hurt optimization, but does not establish the claimed general causal mechanism or lasting improvements after convergence.

The supplementary calibration experiment uses 30% labeled data for fitting and validation but lacks the essential baseline of predicting test accuracy from the labeled sample's empirical accuracy. Its small errors on a random held-out split therefore do not establish practical benefit. Reproducibility is also limited by unspecified domain/reference token lists, incomplete downstream evaluation protocols, and an unidentified Python training corpus.

strengths: The empirical survey covers multiple model families, sizes, and text domains, providing useful evidence of a negative association between perplexity and dispersion within perplexity-conditioned groups.

The appendices add meaningful supporting analyses, including Vendi scores, multilingual benchmarks, held-out calibration, and 30 OLMo checkpoints. These extend the evidence beyond the main illustrative experiments.
The proposed statistics and auxiliary objective are simple. Table 2 reports consistent early-training perplexity improvements, with larger gains in the mixed text/code setting.
weaknesses: The geometric interpretation is stronger than the statistic supports. For normalized vectors u_i, Equation 1 equals N/(N−1) times (1−||mean(u_i)||²). It therefore measures the normalized centroid’s magnitude, not dimensionality or uniform coverage: equally populated antipodal clusters maximize it despite having rank one. The cross-domain objective similarly reduces to separating domain means and can favor within-domain collapse. The Vendi experiments provide complementary empirical evidence but do not resolve these limitations of the proposed metric and loss.

Section 3.1 does not demonstrate label-free example ranking or slice discovery. It constructs batches using known correctness labels and measures a batch-level statistic; no individual scoring procedure or prospective ranking evaluation is supplied. Appendix B.1.3 requires labeled calibration data and lacks the basic baseline of estimating test accuracy directly from the random labeled subset. Repeating label-conditioned mixtures on other datasets also does not establish transfer of a fixed predictor under distribution shift.

The model-selection claims contain concrete numerical contradictions. Section 3.2 claims perfect ranking of nine Qwen checkpoints, but Tables 9–10 contain eight and show cross-size reversals. Using Table 9 and the stated definition, Qwen2.5-1.5B has G=2.1337 at 35.0% accuracy, whereas Distill-Qwen-14B has G=2.2074 at 93.9%, below Distill-Qwen-1.5B’s G=2.6420 at 83.9%. Table 12 also gives CodeLlama-7B a lower cosine gap than Llama2-7B despite higher accuracy. The narrower within-size observations are useful, but the broader ranking and metric-robustness claims need correction.

The retrieval application is not validated end to end. Section 3.3 reports dispersion for only the final block’s attention and FFN outputs, without reporting kNN-LM perplexity, selection regret, or a search across layers. Agreement with a previously reported preference for attention outputs does not establish that maximizing dispersion identifies the best retrieval representation.

The training evidence is preliminary: GPT-2-small trained from scratch is evaluated only at 500 and 1,000 steps, without training-seed uncertainty, convergence results, or comparisons against existing contrastive/repulsive regularizers such as ContraCLM. The squeeze ablation shows that an opposing regularizer can hurt optimization, but does not isolate dispersion as the causal driver of predictive quality.

The central correlations are computed after sorting by perplexity, aggregating into bins, and selecting bins across perplexity space. These are legitimate descriptive associations, but they do not establish individual-level predictive accuracy or robustness to token identity, topic composition, and binning choices. Query-text perplexity is also an inadequate substitute for answer confidence or predictive entropy in the hardness comparisons. Overall, the interesting observations are insufficiently connected to validated practical benefits for acceptance.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant question using a simple, inexpensive geometric statistic. Correlation experiments span several model families, domains, model sizes, and context lengths.
The appendices add useful evidence, including held-out data, Vendi-score comparisons, multilingual benchmarks, and training trajectories.

The auxiliary objective produces consistent early-training perplexity improvements across the reported learning rates, particularly in the cross-domain setting. The reverse-sign ablation provides an additional intervention.
weaknesses: The model-selection claims contradict the reported numbers. Section 3.2 claims perfect ranking of nine checkpoints and Spearman correlation above 0.95, whereas Tables 9–10 contain eight checkpoints. Applying the stated gap formula to those tables yields correlations of approximately 0.43 for Euclidean distance and 0.14 for cosine distance across checkpoints. Within-scale rankings are more favorable, but do not support the stated broader claim. Table 12 also shows a smaller cosine gap for CodeLlama-7B than Llama2-7B despite substantially better accuracy.

The hardness experiments establish aggregate associations in slices constructed using correctness labels, not label-free ranking of individual examples. No individual scoring rule, error-detection AUROC, or prospective slice-discovery evaluation is provided. Appendix B.1.3 adds supervised calibration, but lacks the simple baseline of estimating test accuracy from calibration-set accuracy. Query-text perplexity is also a weaker comparison than answer confidence or predictive entropy.

The kNN-LM application is not evaluated end to end. Section 3.3 and Appendix B.3 compare dispersion between two final-block sublayers but report no resulting retrieval-augmented perplexities. Agreement with an existing attention-versus-FFN observation does not establish that maximizing dispersion selects the best retrieval layer.

The geometric interpretation is too strong. For normalized vectors u_i, the proposed statistic equals N/(N−1) times (1−||mean(u_i)||²), so it measures mean-direction cancellation rather than representation dimensionality or uniformly broad coverage. Two balanced antipodal clusters can maximize it while remaining one-dimensional. The Vendi-score correlations are useful empirical checks but do not establish the claimed general equivalence to embedding breadth or discriminative capacity.

The central perplexity correlations are measured after sorting examples by perplexity, aggregating into bins, and selecting bins uniformly over perplexity. These results do not establish predictive performance on naturally sampled individual examples or across models. Controls for token identity, frequency, topic, and formatting, together with sensitivity to binning, are needed. The explanation also conflates low observed-token perplexity with low predictive entropy.

Training evidence is limited to GPT-2 small trained from scratch for 1,000 steps, with no reported variation across training seeds, convergence results, or comparisons against existing contrastive and isotropy regularizers. Appendix B.4.3 acknowledges the close connection to prior objectives but supplies no empirical comparison. These experiments support preliminary optimization benefits more strongly than general improvements in language-model quality.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code-availability footnote has no link, domain/reference token sets are unspecified, and the model-selection evaluation protocols and Python training corpus are insufficiently documented. Together with the numerical inconsistencies and unvalidated applications, these issues put the paper below the acceptance threshold despite its promising empirical observations.
